paragraphs: Distribution regression estimates how an entire response distribution changes with its predictors. This paper studies conditional deep generative models for responses represented in a high-dimensional space but concentrated near a potentially lower-dimensional manifold. That setting matters because the number of recorded coordinates can greatly exceed the dimension of the underlying structure.

The authors analyze a likelihood-based estimator called a sieve maximum likelihood estimator. They establish large-sample convergence rates for conditional distribution estimation using Hellinger and Wasserstein measures of discrepancy. The rates depend on the intrinsic dimension and smoothness of the true conditional distribution, providing a statistical explanation for how these models can avoid dependence on the full ambient dimension.

The analysis also covers a broader class of nearly singular conditional distributions and highlights the importance of adding a small noise perturbation when observations lie sufficiently close to a manifold. Numerical studies on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate implementation of the approach and complement the theory. The dimensionality advantage is therefore tied to the distribution's underlying structure.
icml-2025-a-likelihood-based-approach-to.tldr: Likelihood-based conditional generative models achieve convergence rates governed by intrinsic dimension and smoothness when responses concentrate near lower-dimensional structure.

paragraphs: As rodents learn to navigate, their place fields change in characteristic ways: more fields appear near rewards, fields stretch against the direction of travel, and individual fields change their spatial selectivity despite stable behavior. This paper asks whether these observations can arise from a common objective: improving navigation to obtain rewards.

The model represents locations using Gaussian radial basis functions, whose amplitudes, centers, and widths determine the place fields. These representations connect directly to an actor-critic system for learning a navigation policy. A temporal difference error drives online updates to both the fields and their downstream connections, allowing the representation and behavior to adapt together at every time step.

The authors show that this framework reproduces the three observed patterns within one reward-maximization account. They also demonstrate improved policy convergence when navigating toward a single target and relearning multiple new targets. The contribution is a normative explanation of why such reorganization could be useful, together with testable predictions, rather than a demonstration that this is the biological mechanism.
icml-2025-a-model-of-place-field-reorgan.tldr: A reward-maximizing navigation model reproduces three place-field reorganization patterns and shows how they can improve policy learning.

paragraphs: This paper develops a greedy search procedure for learning ancestral graphs from complex nonlinear and categorical data. These graphs allow both directed edges and bidirected edges, with the latter representing relationships arising from unobserved variables. Including this second edge type lets the search account for dependencies that involve hidden factors.

The method estimates a normalized likelihood score using multivariate information from selected groups of vertices. The relevant groups are called ac-connected subsets: their vertices connect through collider paths restricted to the group's ancestor set. This construction determines which collections of variables contribute information to the graph score, rather than relying only on isolated pairs.

To keep computation manageable, the algorithm works in two steps, using local information around nodes first and around edges second. It restricts the included information contributions to subsets containing paths with up to two colliders. Despite this explicit restriction, the authors report better performance than state-of-the-art causal discovery methods on challenging benchmark datasets. The result supports the practical value of this localized scoring strategy in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-an-efficient-search-and-score-.tldr: A local multivariate-information scoring method makes greedy ancestral-graph search efficient and outperforms leading causal discovery methods on challenging benchmarks.

paragraphs: Schrödinger bridges provide a framework for generative modeling, including translation between domains without paired examples. Much of the existing work concerns continuous spaces. This paper addresses the theoretical and computational questions that arise when data instead consist of discrete categories, such as text tokens, atom categories, or entries in an image autoencoder's codebook.

The authors build on Iterative Markovian Fitting, an iterative procedure for solving bridge problems. Their central theoretical contribution justifies convergence of its discrete-time version to a Schrödinger bridge in discrete spaces. This supplies a mathematical foundation for using the procedure with categorical representations rather than simply transferring a continuous-space method without justification.

From that foundation, they develop a practical algorithm called Categorical Schrödinger Bridge Matching. Experiments use synthetic data and vector-quantized image representations to demonstrate its performance. The paper therefore connects a convergence result to an implemented generative modeling method. Text and molecular categories motivate the broader setting, while the stated experimental evidence concerns synthetic examples and image representations.
icml-2025-categorical-schrodinger-bridge.tldr: Categorical Schrödinger Bridge Matching turns a convergence result for discrete iterative fitting into a practical generative modeling algorithm.

paragraphs: CFPT targets two sources of information that the authors identify as insufficiently explored in long-term forecasting: relationships between frequency components and recurring patterns in timestamps. Its design treats these as complementary forecasting inputs. One describes interactions within the signal's frequency representation, while the other describes how observations are organized in recurring periods.

The cross-frequency interaction branch processes signals in the frequency domain and combines their features to learn relationships between components. The periodic-aware timestamp branch reshapes timestamp sequences into two-dimensional periodic tensors. It then applies two-dimensional convolution to capture dependencies within a period and correlations across periods, using the timestamp patterns as the organizing structure.

This combination matters because the forecasting model can use both interacting frequency information and repeated temporal organization. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world benchmarks report state-of-the-art long-term forecasting performance. Those results support the combined CFPT approach on the evaluated tasks; the abstract presents the two branches as its main methodological contributions without assigning a separate numerical gain to either one.
icml-2025-cfpt-empowering-time-series-fo.tldr: CFPT combines cross-frequency feature interactions with periodic timestamp modeling to achieve state-of-the-art results on long-term forecasting benchmarks.

paragraphs: Standard attention scores input pairs by projecting them into lower-dimensional queries and keys and taking dot products. This saves computation but can discard information on tasks with intrinsically high-dimensional inputs. It also applies the same scoring rule to every pair, without explicitly allocating computation according to how far apart tokens are.

The paper replaces that scoring function with efficient structured matrices, including Block Tensor-Train and Multi-Level Low Rank matrices. These structures support high-rank scoring or computation that depends on token distance. The aim is to change attention's built-in assumptions while retaining computational efficiency, making the scoring mechanism better suited to the task's information requirements.

On the studied high-dimensional in-context regression tasks, the proposed functions outperform standard attention at any fixed compute budget. For language modeling, where locality patterns matter, the Multi-Level Low Rank method improves scaling laws relative to standard and sliding-window attention. The authors also place both constructions within a broader matrix family, showing a shared way to encode these different computational preferences.
icml-2025-customizing-the-inductive-bias.tldr: Efficient structured matrices let attention preserve high-dimensional information or favor nearby tokens, improving results on regression and language-modeling tasks.

paragraphs: Kernel density estimation here means estimating the sum of a query point's kernel similarities to a dataset. The paper studies a dynamic version of this problem: new data points arrive over time, and estimates for a set of query points need to stay current. The central task is maintaining these estimates efficiently as the collection grows.

The authors introduce a data structure for that maintenance problem and then use it to maintain a sparse approximation of the dataset's fully connected similarity graph. A fully connected graph represents similarities between every pair of points; the sparse approximation provides a smaller graph representation. Connecting density estimation to graph maintenance makes the first data structure useful for a broader computational task.

Building on the maintained graph, the paper develops a fast dynamic spectral clustering algorithm. The authors evaluate their algorithms on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The contribution is thus a sequence of linked methods, from updating kernel sums to maintaining a graph and performing clustering, specifically in the setting where data points are added over time.
icml-2025-dynamic-similarity-graph-const.tldr: A dynamic kernel-density data structure supports sparse similarity-graph maintenance and fast spectral clustering as new points arrive.

paragraphs: Sequential neural activity, in which neurons become active one after another, is one proposed way to maintain short-term information. Recurrent connections can generate such sequences, but this leaves open which dynamical mechanisms support them. This paper identifies two mechanisms that can produce sequence-based short-term memory in recurrent neural networks.

One uses slow-point manifolds to generate sequences directly. The other uses limit cycles that approximate the needed sequence over a localized period of time. Through analytical models, the authors identify properties that govern which mechanism is selected. They also derive how critical learning rates scale with the delay length in delayed cue-discrimination tasks, identifying thresholds beyond which learning is impossible in the analyzed setting.

The authors empirically check these results by training and evaluating approximately 80,000 recurrent networks and making them available for further analysis. The work links the dynamics that maintain information to the conditions under which training can discover them. It also offers experimentally testable neuroscience predictions, extending the relevance of the analysis beyond the trained network collection.
icml-2025-dynamical-phases-of-short-term.tldr: The paper identifies two dynamical mechanisms for short-term memory and derives delay-dependent learning-rate thresholds, supported by approximately 80,000 trained RNNs.

paragraphs: Latent image generators first compress images with an autoencoder, then learn to generate within that compressed space. This paper identifies a problem with existing autoencoders: transformations such as rotation or scaling do not produce corresponding, consistent changes in their latent representations. The resulting latent space becomes more complex for the generative model to learn.

EQ-VAE adds regularization that encourages this transformation consistency, known as equivariance. The authors fine-tune pretrained autoencoders so that their latent representations respond more predictably to transformations that preserve semantic content. They report that this reduces latent-space complexity without degrading reconstruction quality, addressing the representation used by the generator rather than only modifying the generator itself.

The approach improves several generative models, including DiT, SiT, REPA, and MaskGIT. The abstract reports a sevenfold speedup for DiT-XL/2 after just five epochs of SD-VAE fine-tuning. EQ-VAE also works with continuous and discrete autoencoders. Together, these findings show that improving the organization of the compressed representation can benefit multiple kinds of latent image generation.
icml-2025-eq-vae-equivariance-regularize.tldr: EQ-VAE regularizes autoencoder representations to transform consistently with images, improving latent generation without degrading reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: A model can satisfy a fairness objective during training without maintaining that behavior on unseen data. This paper studies that gap as fairness overfitting. The motivation is that many fairness interventions alter training through regularization or other mechanisms, yet do not provide formal guarantees about whether the resulting fairness will generalize.

The authors develop an information-theoretic framework for bounding fairness generalization error. Their bounding technique uses the Efron–Stein inequality and yields bounds involving both mutual information and conditional mutual information. These quantities provide ways to characterize information dependence relevant to the learning process, connecting that dependence to the difference between training and unseen-data fairness.

Empirical evaluations across diverse fairness-aware learning algorithms support the tightness and practical relevance of the bounds. The contribution is therefore both analytical and diagnostic: it supplies a formal way to study fairness overfitting and evidence that the bounds are informative in practice. The framework offers guidance for designing algorithms with better fairness generalization, without itself establishing that every fairness intervention will generalize.
icml-2025-fairness-overfitting-in-machin.tldr: Information-theoretic bounds characterize how fairness achieved during training can fail to generalize, with empirical support across fairness-aware algorithms.

paragraphs: Simultaneous speech translation must decide how long to listen before translating each part of an utterance. Waiting provides more context, but translation must proceed while the speaker is still talking. Hibiki addresses this timing problem with a decoder-only model that processes source and target speech through synchronized streams and jointly produces text and audio tokens.

The training method uses an existing text translation system's perplexity to identify suitable delays for individual words. This weak supervision creates aligned synthetic data that teach the model when to produce translations. After supervised training, Hibiki adapts its translation timing using ordinary temperature sampling, bringing the timing behavior into the model's learned generation process.

On a French-English simultaneous translation task, the authors report state-of-the-art translation quality, speaker fidelity, and naturalness. The simple inference procedure is also compatible with batched translation and real-time deployment on a device. These findings connect the training alignment strategy to a practical system that handles both what to translate and when to speak.
icml-2025-high-fidelity-simultaneous-spe.tldr: Hibiki learns word-level translation delays and jointly generates text and speech, achieving state-of-the-art results on French-English simultaneous translation.

paragraphs: Multi-exit networks attach classifiers inside a backbone so that prediction can finish before the full network has run. Their training commonly follows one of two strategies: train the backbone and exit classifiers jointly, or train the classifiers separately. This paper examines how that choice affects learning, an issue often left unjustified when an early-exit method is introduced.

The authors develop metrics for studying training dynamics and guiding strategy selection. Their analysis finds that the conventional joint and disjoint regimes produce suboptimal performance in the evaluated settings. They propose a mixed strategy that first trains the backbone and then trains the complete multi-exit network, including both the backbone and its internal classifiers.

Evaluations span different architectures, datasets, and early-exit methods, exposing strengths and weaknesses of the training alternatives. The mixed strategy produces consistent improvements in performance and efficiency across these evaluations. The practical message is that early-exit behavior depends on the training schedule as well as the network design, and that a staged approach can improve the resulting system.
icml-2025-how-to-train-your-multi-exit-m.tldr: Training the backbone first and then the whole multi-exit network consistently improves performance and efficiency in the paper's evaluations.

paragraphs: Comparing polygonal curves requires a dissimilarity measure that handles how points along different curves correspond. The paper introduces k-Dynamic Time Warping, or k-DTW, as an alternative to Dynamic Time Warping and Fréchet distance. It establishes stronger metric properties than DTW and greater robustness to outliers than Fréchet distance.

The authors provide exact and approximate algorithms based on parametric search for the kth-largest matched distance. Beyond computation, they prove dimension-free learning bounds for curves. For learning a median curve, some sample-size factors that depend on curve complexity m under DTW are replaced by k, making the choice of dissimilarity consequential for statistical learning.

They also establish strictly smaller bounds on associated Rademacher and Gaussian complexities, with an improvement factor of approximately the square root of m, up to logarithmic factors, when k is much smaller than m. Experiments illustrate benefits for clustering and nearest-neighbor classification. The work thus combines a new curve comparison measure, algorithms for evaluating it, and learning guarantees explaining advantages in particular parameter regimes.
icml-2025-improved-learning-via-k-dtw-a-.tldr: k-DTW offers improved curve-comparison properties and dimension-free learning bounds, with statistical advantages over DTW when k is small relative to curve complexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when an objective is neither smooth nor convex and the algorithm must satisfy differential privacy. It considers both objectives defined by observed data and objectives defined by an underlying population. The target is a Goldstein-stationary point, an approximate stationarity criterion appropriate to this setting, rather than a guarantee of finding a global optimum.

The authors first provide a single-pass algorithm with an explicit sufficient dataset size for achieving the desired stationarity and privacy parameters. Its sample requirement improves on the cited prior method by a factor of at least the square root of the dimension. This matters because increasing dimension can otherwise make the data needed for private optimization particularly demanding.

A second algorithm uses multiple passes and runs in polynomial time, further improving the sample-complexity bound. Its construction combines a sample-efficient empirical optimization method with a proof that Goldstein stationarity transfers from empirical loss to population loss. These results give improved sufficient data requirements, while distinguishing what can be achieved with one pass from what repeated access enables.
icml-2025-improved-sample-complexity-for.tldr: New single-pass and multi-pass differentially private algorithms reduce the sufficient sample sizes for finding Goldstein-stationary points in nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn continuous-time Markov models from data by recovering spectral information about their infinitesimal generator. This generator describes the process's local time evolution, but its unbounded nature makes standard regression and operator-analysis methods difficult to apply. Existing approaches can also be expensive or lack recovery guarantees when observations have small time lags.

The proposed method works through the generator's resolvent, characterized using a Laplace transform of transfer operators. This changes the object being learned while retaining access to the generator's spectral information. The authors report robustness to variations in time lag, including accurate eigenvalue learning when that lag is small.

Their statistical analysis applies to a broader class of Markov processes than current methods, and the approach reduces computational complexity from quadratic to linear in state dimension. Experiments demonstrate the theoretical findings. The combined contribution addresses both the mathematical difficulty of learning the generator and the computational burden associated with high-dimensional states, while improving the treatment of closely spaced observations.
icml-2025-laplace-transform-based-low-co.tldr: Learning a Markov generator through its resolvent supports small-time-lag eigenvalue recovery while reducing computational complexity to linear in state dimension.

paragraphs: This paper treats social-network intervention as an optimization problem over the weights governing user interactions. Such weights can represent how shared content is ranked in feeds. The objective can measure outcomes such as polarization, allowing the intervention to be selected by optimization rather than relying on a handcrafted rule.

The formulation assumes that users' opinions evolve according to the Friedkin-Johnsen model. Under that model, choosing interaction weights leads to a large optimization problem with nonconvex constraints. The authors develop a gradient-based algorithm that can accommodate different objectives, including potentially nonconvex ones, making the framework adaptable to more than one intervention goal.

Experiments solve problems with 4.8 million variables based on Reddit, LiveJournal, and DBLP datasets. The method outperforms competing approaches in computation time and disagreement reduction. These findings support its scalability and effectiveness for the modeled intervention problems. The opinion-dynamics assumption is central to their interpretation: the optimized weights are evaluated through that specified account of how interaction affects opinions.
icml-2025-optimizing-social-network-inte.tldr: A gradient-based method optimizes social interaction weights under Friedkin-Johnsen opinion dynamics, improving speed and disagreement reduction on large intervention problems.

paragraphs: Orthus generates sequences that interleave images and text from inputs that can also mix these modalities. Its central design combines discrete text tokens with continuous image features within an autoregressive framework. Keeping visual features continuous minimizes information loss, while the sequential formulation makes relationships between image and text content straightforward to model.

The model uses two output heads: a language-modeling head predicts text tokens, and a diffusion head generates image features. To construct a base model, the authors replace hard vector quantization in an existing unified autoregressive model with a soft alternative, add the diffusion head, and tune the new modules for image reconstruction. They report an example requiring 72 A100 GPU hours.

Further post-training enables lengthy interleaved image-text outputs. With seven billion parameters, Orthus achieves a GenEval score of 0.58 and an MME-P score of 1265.8, outperforming compared baselines including Show-o and Chameleon. These results support the architecture's combination of visual understanding and generation, while the extended outputs indicate potential for more intricate multimodal tasks.
icml-2025-orthus-autoregressive-interlea.tldr: Orthus combines autoregressive text prediction with a diffusion image head to generate interleaved image-text sequences using continuous visual features.

paragraphs: Forecasting models often train with losses such as mean squared error, which compare predictions and observations one time step at a time. Such comparisons do not directly measure the relationships among nearby values. This paper proposes a patch-wise structural loss that evaluates local segments of a series to capture discrepancies in their temporal structure.

The loss uses local statistical properties, including correlation, variance, and mean. These provide complementary views of whether a predicted patch aligns with the observed patch's structure. By comparing groups of time steps, the objective gives training information about patterns that isolated point comparisons can overlook, while retaining a direct connection to the forecasted values.

The proposed loss can be combined with a point-wise loss, addressing structural mismatch and individual prediction errors together. Extensive experiments report significant improvements for state-of-the-art forecasting models across diverse real-world datasets. The contribution concerns the training objective, offering a way to improve existing models by changing how forecast errors are measured rather than requiring a particular new forecasting architecture.
icml-2025-patch-wise-structural-loss-for.tldr: Patch-wise structural loss compares local correlation, variance, and mean to improve time-series forecasts alongside conventional point-wise error losses.

paragraphs: This paper studies AUC optimization when only positive and unlabeled training examples are available and the test inputs follow a different distribution. It assumes covariate shift: input frequencies can change, but the conditional distribution of labels given inputs stays the same. Ordinary importance weighting for test-risk minimization does not by itself solve the AUC objective considered here.

The authors derive two estimators of test AUC risk. One uses importance-weighted positive and unlabeled data from the training distribution. The other combines importance-weighted training positives with unlabeled examples from the test distribution. A classifier is trained by minimizing a weighted combination of these estimators, which approximates the test AUC risk.

The method requires neither negative labels nor class-prior values, making its data requirements different from the existing importance-weighting approach described in the abstract. Evaluations on six real-world datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The result is a targeted way to learn an AUC-oriented classifier from incomplete labels under a specific distribution-shift assumption, using unlabeled target data to inform the test-distribution objective.
icml-2025-positive-unlabeled-auc-maximiz.tldr: Two test-AUC risk estimators enable learning under covariate shift from positive and unlabeled data without negative labels or class priors.

paragraphs: Image autoregressive models can match leading diffusion models in image quality while generating faster, but those benefits leave a separate question about training-data privacy. This paper compares their privacy exposure through attacks that detect training membership, infer dataset membership, and extract training examples. The analysis uses diffusion models as reference points.

The new membership attack identifies training images with an 86.38% true-positive rate at a 1% false-positive rate, compared with 6.38% for comparable diffusion-model attacks. Building on that attack, dataset inference can detect membership with as few as six samples, versus 200 in the diffusion comparison. These results show substantially more detectable training information in the evaluated autoregressive models.

The authors also extract hundreds of training examples, including 698 from VAR-d30. Together, the findings suggest a privacy-utility trade-off: strong quality and speed accompany greater empirical vulnerability in these comparisons. The evidence establishes a substantial concern for the tested models, while the abstract frames the broader trade-off as suggested by the results rather than as a universal theorem.
icml-2025-privacy-attacks-on-image-autor.tldr: The evaluated image autoregressive models leak substantially more training information than comparable diffusion models through membership inference and training-example extraction.

paragraphs: Composed image retrieval searches using a reference image plus text describing a desired change. Standard contrastive training treats the designated target as positive and other batch images as negatives. Some of those other images may also satisfy the query, so training can incorrectly penalize relevant alternatives and produce a less useful overall result list.

QuRe addresses this issue through a reward-model objective intended to reduce false negatives. It also introduces a hard-negative sampling rule based on the relevance ranking: images are selected between two steep drops in relevance scores after the target. This strategy aims to filter false negatives while identifying challenging examples for training.

The authors introduce HP-FashionIQ to evaluate human preferences beyond whether the single designated target is retrieved. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on FashionIQ and CIRR, plus the strongest alignment with human preferences on HP-FashionIQ. The contribution therefore connects a change in training-example selection with a broader evaluation of retrieval usefulness, where relevant alternatives matter alongside the target image.
icml-2025-qure-query-relevant-retrieval-.tldr: QuRe reduces false-negative training signals in composed image retrieval and improves benchmark performance and alignment with human preferences.

paragraphs: Cell lineage trees describe how cells descend from earlier cells during development. Genetic tracing can reveal these histories, but it is infeasible or ethically constrained in many organisms. This paper instead studies reconstruction from measured cell characteristics, including molecular profiles available through single-cell technologies, using limited information about the true lineage.

CellTreeQM uses a transformer to learn an embedding whose geometry is suited to tree reconstruction. The key formulation is tree-metric learning: the representation is trained so that distances support inference of lineage relationships. The authors systematically examine weakly supervised settings with different amounts of information, making the supervision requirement part of the study.

They also introduce a benchmark containing synthetic data generated through Brownian motion with independent noise and spurious signals, together with lineage-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. Experiments show recovery of lineage structure with minimal supervision and limited data. The work presents a scalable reconstruction framework and, to the authors' knowledge, the first explicit metric-learning formulation of cell lineage inference.
icml-2025-reconstructing-cell-lineage-tr.tldr: CellTreeQM learns representations suited to lineage-tree reconstruction and recovers cell relationships with minimal supervision and limited data in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper asks how accurately Fisher information can be estimated after an unknown density is smoothed with Gaussian noise. The observations are independent and identically distributed, and the original density is assumed to have compact support and Hölder smoothness. The smoothing variance t is central: the authors track precisely how estimation difficulty changes with it.

They derive a minimax rate, describing the best worst-case estimation accuracy over the specified density class, including sharp dependence on t. For positive smoothing variance, some simple plug-in estimators attain that rate. This is consequential because extra debiasing steps are widely used to attain sharp rates in the unsmoothed setting, whereas these smoothed estimators can be optimal without those additions.

The precise dependence on smoothing also yields results for mutual information and entropy estimation. Through the I-MMSE and de Bruijn identities, the authors show that plug-in estimators achieve the parametric rate. The findings thus connect smoothing to both simpler optimal Fisher-information estimation and sharp guarantees for related information quantities.
icml-2025-sharp-optimality-of-simple-plu.tldr: For Gaussian-smoothed densities under the stated regularity assumptions, simple plug-in estimators achieve sharp optimal Fisher-information estimation rates.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether hidden features learned by a model can be recovered efficiently from an agent's feedback. The feedback consists of relative triplet comparisons, providing comparative judgments rather than direct access to the feature matrix. The features may describe dictionaries in language models or components associated with a learned distance function.

The authors analyze how much feedback is needed when the feature structure is sparse. They distinguish two access settings. When the agent can construct activations, they establish tight complexity bounds. When feedback is restricted to distributional information, they establish strong upper bounds in sparse scenarios. This distinction matters because the available form of interaction changes what recovery guarantees can be established.

Experiments test the theory in two applications: recovering features from models trained with Recursive Feature Machines and extracting dictionaries from sparse autoencoders trained on large language models. The contribution links sparse feature recovery to an explicit accounting of feedback requirements, with empirical validation in both applications. The guarantees remain differentiated by the agent's access and the sparsity setting.
icml-2025-the-complexity-of-learning-spa.tldr: The paper bounds the comparison feedback needed to recover sparse hidden features, with guarantees that depend on the agent's access to activations.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis concerns sparse subnetworks that retain the predictive performance of a larger network. For graph neural networks, evidence has largely been empirical. This paper develops theory around expressivity: whether a sparse network can still distinguish graphs with different structures. Losing that ability can undermine what the network is capable of predicting.

The authors establish conditions under which a sparsely initialized graph neural network matches the expressivity of the full network, particularly relative to the Weisfeiler-Leman test. Within this setting, they formulate and prove a Strong Expressive Lottery Ticket Hypothesis. The result identifies circumstances in which sparsity preserves a crucial representational capability.

They further show that greater expressivity at initialization can potentially accelerate convergence and improve generalization. Examples from drug discovery illustrate the findings. The contribution therefore connects sparse initialization, graph distinguishability, and learning behavior, while retaining the conditional nature of the guarantees. Matching expressivity is established under specified conditions, and the convergence and generalization benefits are presented as potential consequences.
icml-2025-weisfeiler-and-leman-go-gambli.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for sparse GNNs to preserve full-network expressivity and links expressive initialization to potential learning benefits.
